idiom_name: a = b.also { b = a } (stdlib also) plus JVM reference rebinding
implementation_notes: Kotlin has no swap in the language or the standard library, and the official idioms page settles it with a scope function: `a = b.also { b = a }` (also calls the block with its receiver and returns the receiver, so b's old value is captured before b is overwritten) replaces both the temporary variable and the whole C++ protocol - there is no noexcept, no ADL and no customization point, and reference assignment can neither allocate nor throw. For a class, keep the state behind one var property or backing field and exchange it; on the JVM java.util.Collections.swap(list, i, j) is available for lists and java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicReference for atomic publication. Data classes and val properties are values rather than handles: when the state is immutable, publish a new instance instead of swapping fields.
pitfalls: The also idiom is only correct in the written order: `a = b.also { b = a }` captures b's old value, while reversing it (`b = a.also { a = b }`) makes both variables equal.

Custom property setters, delegated properties and observable state holders run code on assignment and can throw; if the commit must not fail, exchange backing fields or state references rather than setters.
Locals captured by a lambda are boxed into Ref objects, so "swapping" captured vars through a closure allocates; perform the exchange in the enclosing function instead.
Two AtomicReferences cannot be exchanged atomically as a pair: for shared state keep everything that must change together in one AtomicReference to an immutable holder.
